PSI UPSILON ARCHIVES
HAVE A NEW HOME
By Peter A. GaBau
IT
IS very doubtful if any other
fraternity has as many archives
as Psi Upsilon has in its new Archive
Room at the Executive Council
ofiices in New York. This room was
formally opened on November 6,
1939, when it was visited by mem
bers of the Executive Council under
the leadership of Scott Turner, Phi
'02, President of the Council.
During the past century, many
of our brethren have cooperated in
sending records of events or me
mentos to certain loyal members
who have had a responsibility for
fraternity matters. The result has
been that you almost always find
one of the following associated with
the archives in question : Robinson,
Beta '41,, Bridgman, Gamma '66,
Fox, Upsilon '67, Smiley, Xi '74,
Coleman, Xi '76, Bangs, Lambda
'78, Irwin, Delta '94, Waugh, Pi
'98, Naylor, Zeta '09, Corcoran,
Omega '15 and more recently, Kent,
Delta Delta '11, A. C. Jacobs, Phi
'21 (son of the late Albert Poole
Jacobs, Phi '73).
In addition to the above, there
are two brothers who have been out
standing, Albert Poole Jacobs, Phi
'73, and Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi
'93. Brother Jacobs was the Editor
of the Psi Upsilon Epitome, a his
tory of the first fifty years of Psi
Upsilon. His records and archives
cannot be duplicated. They were so
appreciated by the Executive Coun
cil that it purchased them about
25 years ago for our archives.
Brother Jacobs was the Baird* of
yesteryear.

The other brother to whom I refer
is Earl D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, who
was associated with Brother Jacobs
back in 1893, when the latter
early planted the archive seed in
Brother Babst. Today he has scrapbooks containing material of many
great Psi U occasions from 1889
to 1939. In addition. Brother Babst
is actively interested in contribut
ing to the National Fraternity
Archive Project now under consid
eration at the University of Michi
gan at Ann Arbor.
Brother Babst's collection sug
gests to us that there must be many
other collections of one type or
another, which, at the proper time,
might well be included for safekeep
ing in our archives.
Any reference to our archives
would not be complete without pay
ing tribute to the tireless efforts of
Herbert L. Bridgman, Gamma '66,
for many decades President of the
Executive Council. Being very me
ticulous about any printed material,
he made sure that it was properly
recorded as to date, place and func
tion. As the result, we have an
abundance of factual archives bear
ing his signature.
The new Archive Room is modern
in every respect. Last summer,
through the initiation of Brother
Turner, and with the help of Broth
ers Babst and Collins, Iota '03, we
moved the archives from a Brooklyn
warehouse to New York. In the

PSI U ALUMNI IN CHICAGO
SET NEW DINNER FASHION
LAST
October all Psi U's living
in greater Chicago received in
part the following announcement :
"To Psi U Alumni of all chapters
from the class of 1921 or earlier
(in other words to those brothers
40 years old and older): Greet
ings: A Reunion Dinner but NO
SPEECHES There will doubt
less be other Psi U parties for the
brothers 'old and young' but this is
restricted to . . . those of us who are
40 or more. No, you just cannot af
ford to miss joining in this pleasant
evening. ..."
Even though there are only about
200 Psi U's, residing in the Chicago
area, who can claim they are 40 or
older, and in spite of the fact that
there was only about six days no
tice, about 45 turned out for one of
the best reunions in years.
It was a gala evening�
with no
speeches. From Fred Mehlhop, Phi
'88, down to the youngest brother
present, everyone had a fine evening
renewing old friendships and singing
Psi U songs. The result was so suc
cessful that it was decided to hold
two such gatherings each year for
this group. In addition to those pres
ent, many sent in regrets that other
engagements kept them from attend
ing but that they wanted to be on
hand for the next gathering. Since
the party even more have signified
their desire to be included next time.

PSI UPSILON ALL AMERICAN
FOOTBALL TEAM FOR 1939
By Willis Brown, Omicron '31, of the Minneapolis Star-Journal
THE
third Psi Upsilon All Amer
ican football team presented an
other terrific headache before final
selections were made. As in the
1938 selections, the men were cho
sen on the basis of reports sent by
the various chapters. Like last year's
team, Psi Upsilon's 1939 edition had
a great wealth of good wing material
�
much more than for any other po
sition. But the prospects in the
freshman and pledge classes at the
chapters point to more and better
backfield men in 1940.
Psi Upsilon's first All American,
Amos Alonzo Stagg, Beta '88 (Dia
mond, Nov. 1939), for the third year
is the unanimous choice as honorary
coach. The "Grand Old Man," who
last fall celebrated his 50th anniver
sary as a football mentor, is still
coaching at the College of the Paci
fic in California.
Five colleges and universities are
represented on the 1939 team. This
number is two less than a year ago.
Dartmouth paced the field with four
men, Cornell came second with three
men and Bowdoin, third with two.
California and Wesleyan had one
each.
It was the steady, driving play of
a Dartmouth senior end that ac
counted for the honor of being cho
sen captain of the 1939 Psi Upsilon
All American team. Despite a knee
injury which kept him out of two
games for the Big Green, Charles
(Whit) Miller, of Seattle, Wash.,
stood above the rest of the field.
Whit was also captain of the Dart
mouth team, which had a very suc
cessful season. He played sixty min
utes in the Navy game, and his fine
blocking and defensive play all sea
son made him a valuable man on the
Hanover eleven. The other flank po
sition goes to a Cornell junior: Kirk
Hershey, of Philadelphia. He scored
five touchdowns for the Ithacans
and, with his famed end-around
plays was a constant menace to op
posing teams. He was one of the big
ground gainers for undefeated Cor
nell, called by many sporting ex
perts the outstanding team of 1939.
Two juniors hold down the tackle
posts. Robert O'Brien, of Boston,
was a hard charging tackle playing
in his first year as a regular for Dart
mouth. He stood out many times,
but his outstanding feat of the year
was the blocking of a punt in the
Hampden-Sydney game. William
(Bull) Leckie, of Columbus, 0., was
the strongest man on the strong
est team that Wesleyan has had in
recent years. This 190-pound dyna
miter deserves a notch on the first
team.
Two more juniors were chosen for
the guard positions. Frank Finne
ran, of Harrison, N. Y., who learned
his football last year by under
studying All American Al Van
Ranst, Chi '39, was shifted from his
regular center position to fill a gap
at guard. Frank, one of Cornell's
ironmen, played almost all of every
game. His forte was pass defense.

Louis Alonzo Young, Jr., of Narberth. Pa., is the other guard. He
played for Dartmouth in nearly all
of the Navy, Princeton, and Cornell

The remarkably steady play of
Hack Webster during the past three

enough for placing the Lexington,

Hack was a fierce tackier, a strong

some of his team's victories. Add to
that his interception of a crucial
pass that meant victory for Bow
doin in the Massachusetts State
game and it is easily understood why
Hack was selected for center.
The backfield presented a difficult
problem in making selections. But a
California junior, William (Bill) El
more, came up with the quarterback
post tucked under his belt. Bill was
a consistent player who specialized
in blocking and defensive play. He
makes a logical blocker for the other
three hard-running backs.
Two more juniors were chosen for
the halfback post. One, William J.
Murphy, of Cornell, was an excel
lent passer and kicker, and had
much to do with the Red's unblem
ished record. It is good news for Cor
nell that he still has one season left.
To the other halfback post goes
Henry (Bad News) Bonzagni of
Bowdoin. Henry got his nickname
from his shifty, open field running
which was a constant nightmare for
Bowdoin opponents. Outstanding as
a great climax runner, "Bad News"
scored three touchdowns on runs of
more than 60 yards. In addition, he
was a brilliant passer.
To the fullback goes one of the na
tion's outstanding backs: William
D. (Wild Bill) Hutchinson, a Dart
mouth senior from New York City.
His feature play of the year was
in the Harvard game: seeing that
one of his punts might be blocked he
snaked his way 40 yards down a
broken field to score a touchdown.
Altogether, he scored six touch
downs for Dartmouth last season.

HENRY TOPPING, OMEGA '81, A GREAT
PSI U OF THE FAR EAST
By Ernest W. Clement, Omega '80
{The Foreword is by Herbert S. Houston, Omega '88)
IT
SEEMS that my assignment
as the New York World's Fair
Commissioner to the Far East has
carried with it an assignment from
The Diamond to check up on some
of the Psi U's, past and present, of
the Orient. In the last issue I had
the pleasure of collaborating with
Brother Archie Douglas of the
Lambda and Brother Stoyle of the
Tau in a little article on the famous
Psi U banker, the late Brother
Manzo Kushida, Tau '90. Now I
have been asked by the editors to
bring together an article about
Brother Henry Topping, of my own
Omega chapter, who for nearly
fifty years has been an outstanding
figure in the educational and reli
gious life of Japan. It happens that
he is in this country at present. Con
sequently, I hope this article may be
a means of bringing him in touch
with various Psi U's as he travels
around the United States. Let me
say at once that everyone will find
Brother Topping with a very hearty
Psi U grip, with a
friendly and clear
look in his eyes, and with a most
sound and interesting view of world
affairs both in the East and in the
West.
